content: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin condition primarily affecting the central face, characterized by persistent redness (erythema), flushing, visible blood vessels (telangiectasia), pimples, and sometimes thickened skin. It results from a complex interaction of genetic, vascular, environmental, and immune system factors, causing inflammation and vascular hyperreactivity. Key synonyms include "adult acne" (though this is a misnomer) and "facial redness disorder." While it most commonly affects adults aged 30-50, particularly those with fair skin, rosacea can have varying presentations. Clinically, rosacea includes different subtypes such as erythematotelangiectatic, papulopustular, phymatous, and ocular rosacea. Diagnosis relies on clinical evaluation by a healthcare professional with no definitive laboratory test. Current treatments focus on symptom management, including topical and oral medications targeting inflammation and vascular changes, alongside lifestyle modifications to avoid known triggers like sun exposure, hot beverages, or stress. Importantly, rosacea is not contagious nor caused by poor hygiene, and it has no cure but can be effectively controlled. Safety considerations include potential side effects of medications (e.g., skin irritation, antibiotic resistance) and the need to avoid overuse of harsh skin products. Limitations of current evidence highlight the heterogeneity of rosacea presentations and response variability to treatments, necessitating personalized management plans. This module provides comprehensive, evidence-calibrated education on rosacea to support patient understanding, guide clinical discussions, and inform lifestyle choices that promote skin health and quality of life.

content: Rosacea is a chronic inflammatory skin condition that affects mainly the face. It is marked by episodes of facial redness, visible small blood vessels, bumps resembling acne, and sometimes a thickening or swelling of the skin, especially on the nose (rhinophyma). Rosacea is not contagious and tends to progress slowly over time if untreated. It most commonly impacts the central face including cheeks, nose, forehead, and chin.

content: The exact cause of rosacea is not fully understood. Multiple factors are implicated, including genetic predisposition, abnormalities in facial blood vessels leading to vascular hyperreactivity, immune system dysregulation causing inflammation, presence of skin microorganisms such as Demodex mites, and environmental triggers like ultraviolet light. These factors interplay to cause chronic inflammation and visible facial redness.

content: Risk factors include fair skin phototypes (Fitzpatrick I-III), family history of rosacea, age between 30 and 50 years, female gender (though men often have more severe forms), and environmental exposures such as sun exposure or extreme temperatures. Emotional stress and certain dietary factors also contribute to flare-ups.

content: Common symptoms include transient or persistent facial redness, frequent flushing episodes, visible dilated blood vessels (telangiectasia), appearance of papules and pustules resembling acne, burning or stinging sensations, dry skin, and in some cases, thickened skin especially around the nose. Ocular rosacea involves the eyes with symptoms like irritation, dryness, redness, and swelling.

content: Rosacea is classified into four primary subtypes: 1) Erythematotelangiectatic rosacea characterized by flushing and redness with visible blood vessels, 2) Papulopustular rosacea involving redness with acne-like bumps, 3) Phymatous rosacea leading to skin thickening and swelling often of the nose (rhinophyma), and 4) Ocular rosacea affecting the eyes causing inflammation and irritation. Some patients may present with features of multiple subtypes.

content: Rosacea diagnosis is clinical, based on physical examination of characteristic symptoms. No specific laboratory tests or biopsies are typically needed. Diagnostic criteria include presence of flushing combined with persistent central facial erythema, and/or papules/pustules without comedones. Diagnosis includes excluding other conditions such as acne vulgaris, lupus, or seborrheic dermatitis.

content: Treatment options include topical agents like metronidazole, azelaic acid, ivermectin, and brimonidine which reduce inflammation and redness. Oral antibiotics such as doxycycline are often used for anti-inflammatory effects. Laser and light-based therapies target visible blood vessels and redness. In severe phymatous rosacea, surgical and dermatologic procedures may be warranted. Treatment choice depends on subtype and severity.

content: Patients benefit from identifying and avoiding personalized triggers such as sun exposure, hot drinks, spicy foods, alcohol, and stress. Daily skin care using gentle cleansers and moisturizers avoiding irritants is recommended. Sun protection with broad-spectrum sunscreen is essential. Adequate sleep and stress management may reduce flares. Patient education enhances adherence and symptom control.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Some treatments can cause skin irritation, dryness, or photosensitivity. Oral antibiotics should be used under medical supervision to avoid resistance. Laser treatments require experienced providers to minimize adverse effects. Patients should avoid harsh skin products and overuse of steroids on the face as topical steroids can exacerbate rosacea.

content: Rosacea is often mistaken for acne, allergy, or simply skin redness from poor hygiene, which is untrue. It is not contagious. The belief that it is caused by poor cleanliness or lack of washing is incorrect. Rosacea cannot be cured but can be effectively managed. Some think it only affects women, but men can experience severe disease.

content: Rosacea is a chronic condition with fluctuating severity. While not life-threatening, it can significantly impact mental health causing embarrassment, anxiety, and social withdrawal.
